# RTL Design of the Flexlink Node {#sec-rtl}

The model of @sec-simulink showed that the idea of the data path works. The next step was to turn this idea into real hardware that uses Flexlink, keeps its own data, passes the rest and answers the master. This chapter describes the Verilog design that does this on each GateMate. A GateMate that runs this design is called a *Flexlink node*. Every node in the chain runs the same design. The first node receives the packets from the *master* over the *uplink*, which is the PC in this prototype, and every further node receives them from the node before it. Each node keeps the brightness values of its own segment, forwards all other data, generates the PWM for its four LED channels and sends answers back to the master or to a node before it over the *downlink*. The complete code is available in the repository of this thesis (@sec-appendix-b).

The chapter first gives a short overview of how the design developed (@sec-rtl-path). It then explains the rules that shaped the design and why each of them was chosen (@sec-design-principles). Finally it walks through the design from the top level down to the single blocks.

## Development Path {#sec-rtl-path}

The GateMate and the open-source tool flow were new at the start of this work. The node was therefore built up in small steps, and each step added one new thing to a design that already worked. This section gives only a short overview. The rest of the chapter describes the final design.

The first design made an on-board LED blink, which tested the whole tool flow on the real board. A push button, a running light and LED fading with an 8-bit PWM followed. The 16-bit PWM then needed the PLL, because the 10 MHz board clock gives only 152.6 Hz. Next I implemented a simple communication between two boards. In the first test, board B had no logic at all and only showed the data of board A on its LED. A UART link followed, then board A sent a 16-bit brightness value, and board B decoded it and generated the PWM. The Flexlink parts were then added one by one. The 9-bit receiver and transmitter came first, then the forwarding and finally Count Segments with the answers. The PC first sent one value, then two and then a full segment of eight bytes. At the end the baud rate was raised from 115,200 to 1 MBaud.

## Design Principles {#sec-design-principles}

Following rules guided the design. Each one answers a requirement from @sec-requirements or a problem that the chain would otherwise have.

The first rule is portable code. The design uses only synthesizable Verilog [@ieee1364] with general elements such as registers, counters, comparators and a small memory (@sec-verilog). The only GateMate-specific block is the PLL `CC_PLL` in the top module, and the pin assignment sits in a separate constraint file. This keeps the path to a later ASIC open (R15).

The second rule is one clock domain. All registers run on the 50 MHz system clock `clk_sys`, which the PLL makes from the 10 MHz board oscillator. A single clock keeps the timing simple. Every path has one clock period of 20 ns (@eq-clock-period), the tool checks all paths in one analysis and no data has to cross between clock domains. The value of 50 MHz follows from the PWM and UART requirements (@sec-req-pwm-clock). The PWM outputs stay off until the PLL reports a stable clock, so the LEDs cannot flash random values while the clock starts.

The third rule is safe handling of outside signals. The serial inputs `up_rx` and `dn_rx` come from another device and do not follow the FPGA clock. Each of them therefore passes through a two-flip-flop synchronizer before it is used (@sec-clocking).

The fourth rule is the same design on every node. All GateMates use the same bitstream and the same pin file, and the design contains no fixed node number. Each node learns its ID at run time from the *Count Segments* command coming from previous nodes/ master. Until then, the ID register `my_id` holds 0xFF, which means "not counted yet". Any node can therefore replace any other node without modifying the build (R6).

The fifth rule is cut-through forwarding. A node passes on every word that is not its own as soon as the word has arrived, instead of waiting for the whole packet [@kermani1979]. The reason is the 25 ms limit. Store-and-forward would add a whole packet at every node, while cut-through adds only about one word time (@sec-req-timing). A small first-in-first-out (FIFO) buffer of eight 9-bit words in each direction holds a word while the transmitter is busy, so no word is lost when input and output are not exactly in step (@sec-forwarding).

The sixth rule is that nothing changes before a complete and correct packet. A node takes over new LED levels or a new ID only at the end of a packet (EOP) and only if the packet was complete. LED levels need all eight own data bytes, and a new ID needs exactly one count value. A received word is accepted only if its stop bit is 1. The reason is simple. A broken packet must never leave the LEDs half-updated, for example with a new red value next to an old blue value (@sec-uplink-decoder, @sec-error-handling).

The seventh rule is ordered answers. A node sends its own answer first and then passes on the answers of the nodes behind it, and it never mixes two packets. If it is already passing on a packet from the next node, it finishes that packet before it starts its own answer. The master therefore receives complete answers one after the other and can tell them apart by the ID (@sec-downlink).

The design consists of four modules in one source file (@tbl-modules). All values that might change are constants at the top of the code (@tbl-design-parameters). The baud rate appears only through `CLKS_PER_BIT`, so it can be changed without touching the receiver or the transmitter. At 115,200 baud, for example, the value would be $50{,}000{,}000 / 115{,}200 \approx 434$.

| **Module**       | **Task**                                                                        |
|:-----------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `flexlink_node`  | top module with PLL, uplink decoder, LED registers, PWM generator and downlink logic |
| `uart_rx9`       | receives one 9-bit UART word (used twice, for uplink and downlink)              |
| `uart_tx9`       | sends one 9-bit UART word (used twice, for uplink and downlink)                 |
| `fifo9`          | buffer for eight 9-bit words (used twice, for uplink and downlink)              |

: Modules of the Flexlink node design {#tbl-modules}

| **Name**        | **Type**     | **Value**    | **Meaning**                                                   |
|:----------------|:-------------|:-------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------|
| `CLKS_PER_BIT`  | parameter    | 50           | clock cycles per UART bit ($50\ \text{MHz} / 1\ \text{MBaud}$)|
| `MY_TEMP`       | parameter    | 40 (0x28)    | fixed temperature value sent in the LED answer                |
| `MY_BYTES`      | localparam   | 8            | data bytes kept by each node (4 channels × 16 bit)            |
| `LED_UP_SOP`    | localparam   | 0x100        | start of an LED data packet (uplink)                          |
| `LED_DN_SOP`    | localparam   | 0x180        | start of an LED answer (downlink)                             |
| `CNT_UP_SOP`    | localparam   | 0x160        | start of a Count Segments packet (uplink)                     |
| `CNT_DN_SOP`    | localparam   | 0x1B0        | start of a Count Segments answer (downlink)                   |
| `FL_EOP`        | localparam   | 0x176        | end of packet                                                 |

: Parameters and constants of the Flexlink node design {#tbl-design-parameters}

## Top-Level Architecture {#sec-top-level}

The top module `flexlink_node` connects all parts of the node (@fig-top-level). It holds the PLL, two UART receivers, two UART transmitters and two FIFO buffers. It also holds the logic that decodes the packets, stores the LED levels, generates the PWM and builds the answers. The uplink path runs from `up_rx` to `up_tx`, and the downlink path runs from `dn_rx` to `dn_tx`. The PWM generator takes its values from the uplink path and drives the four LED outputs.

![Block diagram of the top module `flexlink_node`. The uplink path is drawn in blue, the downlink path in red and the PWM path in green.](images/ch5_top_level){#fig-top-level width=100%}

### Clock and Reset {#sec-clock-reset}

The evaluation board provides a 10 MHz clock from its oscillator. The GateMate primitive `CC_PLL` turns it into the 50 MHz system clock `clk_sys`, which drives every register. It is set up with a reference of 10 MHz, an output of 50 MHz and the economy mode (@lst-pll).

```{.verilog #lst-pll lst-cap="Instance of the GateMate PLL in the top module (shortened)"}
CC_PLL #(
    .REF_CLK ("10.0"),
    .OUT_CLK ("50.0"),
    .PERF_MD ("ECONOMY")
) pll_inst (
    .CLK_REF        (clk),
    .USR_PLL_LOCKED (pll_locked),
    .CLK0           (clk_sys)
    // other ports not used
);
```

After power-up, the PLL needs a short time until its output is stable, and it reports this with the signal `pll_locked`. The PWM outputs are held low until then, so the LEDs stay dark while the clock starts.

The design has no separate reset input. Every register gets a start value in its declaration instead, for example `reg [7:0] my_id = 8'hFF;`. When the FPGA is configured, the bitstream loads these values into the flip-flops, and the design starts in a known state. All LED levels are 0, no packet is open and the node has the ID 0xFF. This works on an FPGA because the configuration sets the flip-flops.

### Module Overview {#sec-module-overview}

The top module uses seven instances of four module types. Besides the PLL `pll_inst`, there is one receiver, one FIFO and one transmitter for each direction. On the uplink, `u_up_rx` receives the words from `up_rx`, `u_up_q` holds the words that wait for the transmitter and `u_up_tx` sends them on `up_tx`. The downlink has the same three parts with the names `u_dn_rx`, `u_dn_q` and `u_dn_tx`.

Three more functional blocks are written directly in the top module as `always` blocks. The uplink decoder looks at every word on the uplink. It keeps the eight data bytes that belong to the node, takes the ID from a Count Segments packet and passes all other words on (@sec-uplink-decoder). The downlink logic sends the answer of the node and then passes on the answers from the next node without mixing two packets (@sec-downlink). The PWM generator compares one free-running 16-bit counter with the four stored levels and drives the outputs `seg1` to `seg4` (@sec-pwm-generator). The blocks talk to each other through internal signals. Most of these are short pulses that are 1 for exactly one clock cycle and tell the next block that new data is ready.

### Top-Level Ports {#sec-top-ports}

The ports of `flexlink_node` connect the design to the pins of the FPGA (@tbl-top-ports). They form four groups. These are the clock input, the four serial lines of the chain, the four segment outputs and the outputs for the on-board LEDs.

| **Port**       | **Direction** | **Width** | **Pmod pin** | **Meaning**                                                        |
|:---------------|:--------------|:----------|:-------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `clk`          | input         | 1         | —            | 10 MHz clock from the on-board oscillator, input of the PLL        |
| `up_rx`        | input         | 1         | 1            | uplink in, from the master (first node) or from the previous node  |
| `dn_tx`        | output        | 1         | 2            | downlink out, to the master (first node) or to the previous node   |
| `up_tx`        | output        | 1         | 3            | uplink out, to the next node                                       |
| `dn_rx`        | input         | 1         | 4            | downlink in, from the next node                                    |
| `seg1`         | output        | 1         | 7            | PWM signal of the red channel                                      |
| `seg2`         | output        | 1         | 8            | PWM signal of the green channel                                    |
| `seg3`         | output        | 1         | 9            | PWM signal of the blue channel                                     |
| `seg4`         | output        | 1         | 10           | PWM signal of the white channel                                    |
| `vref_2v5`     | output        | 1         | —            | constant high level, used as a 2.5 V reference on the breadboard   |
| `leds_n[7:0]`  | output        | 8         | —            | on-board LEDs D1 to D8, *active low* (0 means LED on)              |

: Ports of the top module `flexlink_node` {#tbl-top-ports}

The serial ports come in pairs, with one receiver and one transmitter for each direction. On the uplink, `up_rx` receives the packets and `up_tx` sends the forwarded words to the next node. On the downlink, `dn_rx` receives the answers of the next node and `dn_tx` sends them on towards the master together with the node's own answer. Every node uses the same pins, so a chain is built by connecting `up_tx` of one node to `up_rx` of the next and `dn_tx` of the next node back to `dn_rx`.

The last node needs no special design. Its `up_tx` and `dn_rx` are simply left open. A pull-up in the pin file holds the open `dn_rx` high (@sec-hw-flow). High is the idle level of a UART line, so the receiver of the last node never sees a false start bit.

The on-board LEDs are only for checking. They make the state of a node visible without an oscilloscope. D1 to D4 follow the four PWM signals and shine like the external LEDs. D5 to D8 show the lower four bits of `my_id`. Before the first count all four are on, because the ID is 0xFF. After the count, GM1 with ID 00 shows no LED and GM2 with ID 01 shows only D5. The LEDs are active low, so the design drives them with inverted signals.

## UART Receiver and Transmitter {#sec-uart-rxtx}

Each node holds two receivers (`uart_rx9`) and two transmitters (`uart_tx9`), one of each for the uplink and the downlink. Both handle one Flexlink word at a time. A word has nine data bits and travels as an 11-bit frame with one start bit and one stop bit (@sec-9bit-uart). The data bits are sent with the least significant bit (LSB) first. At 1 MBaud one bit lasts 1 µs, which is `CLKS_PER_BIT` = 50 cycles of the system clock.

### Receiver {#sec-uart-rx}

The receiver has to solve two problems. The input comes from another device with its own clock, so it can change at any moment. Each bit must also be read at a moment when it is stable, which is in its middle (@sec-uart).

The first problem is solved by an input synchronizer. The input `rx` passes through two flip-flops in a row, `rx_meta` and `rx_sync` [@ginosar2011]. If the first one samples the line exactly while it changes, it can become metastable for a short time. The second flip-flop gives it one full clock cycle to settle, so the rest of the receiver only sees a clean signal (@sec-clocking). This costs two clock cycles, which is 40 ns and very small next to the bit time of 1 µs.

The second problem is solved by a small finite state machine with four states (@fig-uart-rx-fsm). A counter `clk_cnt` counts the clock cycles inside a bit, and `bit_idx` counts the data bits.

![State machine of the UART receiver `uart_rx9`.](images/ch5_uart_rx_fsm){#fig-uart-rx-fsm width=100%}

In the state IDLE the line is high, and the receiver waits for a falling edge. In START it waits for half a bit, which is 25 cycles, until the middle of the start bit. If the line is still low, a real start bit has arrived and the receiver moves on to DATA. If the line is high again, the edge was only a short glitch, and the receiver returns to IDLE. In DATA it waits one full bit of 50 cycles at a time. Each wait ends in the middle of the next data bit, where the bit is stored at position `bit_idx`. After the ninth bit the receiver moves to STOP. One bit time later it is in the middle of the stop bit. Only if the stop bit is high does the output `valid` become 1 for one clock cycle. A low stop bit means a broken frame, and the word is dropped. In both cases the receiver returns to IDLE.

@lst-uart-rx shows the states DATA and STOP. The bits are stored with `data[bit_idx]`, and `bit_idx` counts up from 0. The first received bit therefore becomes bit 0, which is exactly the LSB-first order of the UART.

```{.verilog #lst-uart-rx lst-cap="DATA and STOP states of the UART receiver uart_rx9"}
DATA:  if (clk_cnt == CLKS_PER_BIT - 1) begin         // middle of each data bit
           clk_cnt       <= 16'd0;
           data[bit_idx] <= rx_sync;
           if (bit_idx == 4'd8) state <= STOP;
           bit_idx <= bit_idx + 4'd1;
       end else clk_cnt <= clk_cnt + 16'd1;

STOP:  if (clk_cnt == CLKS_PER_BIT - 1) begin         // stop bit must be 1
           clk_cnt <= 16'd0;
           state   <= IDLE;
           valid   <= (rx_sync == 1'b1);
       end else clk_cnt <= clk_cnt + 16'd1;
```

The moment when a word is ready matters for the forwarding delay. The `valid` pulse comes in the middle of the stop bit. Counted from the falling edge of the start bit, this is half a start bit, nine data bits and one more bit, so $0.5 + 9 + 1 = 10.5$ bit times (@fig-uart-rx-sampling). The receiver is back in IDLE already at this point, so it is ready for the next start bit even if the next word follows without any gap.

![Sampling of one Flexlink word by the receiver. Each bit is read in its middle, and the word is ready 10.5 bit times after the falling edge of the start bit.](images/ch5_uart_rx_sampling){#fig-uart-rx-sampling width=100%}

The receiver measures the bit times with its own clock, so a small difference between the clocks of sender and receiver adds up over the frame. The last sample, in the stop bit, may move by up to half a bit before it lands in the wrong bit. This allows a total clock difference of about $0.5 / 10.5 \approx 4.8\ \%$. The receiver also synchronises again on the start bit of every word, so the error can never add up over more than one word.

### Transmitter {#sec-uart-tx}

The transmitter is simpler, because it makes the timing itself. When the input `send` is 1 for one clock cycle and the transmitter is free, it loads the whole frame into an 11-bit shift register (@lst-uart-tx).

```{.verilog #lst-uart-tx lst-cap="Loading the frame in the UART transmitter uart_tx9"}
shift     <= {1'b1, data, 1'b0};   // {stop bit, 9 data bits, start bit}
bits_left <= 4'd11;
```

The start bit sits in the lowest position, followed by the nine data bits and the stop bit. The output `tx` always shows the lowest bit of the register. Every 50 clock cycles the register moves one place to the right, so the bits leave as start bit, `data[0]` to `data[8]` and stop bit, which is again LSB first. The signal `busy` is 1 while bits are left to send, and new words are only started when it is 0. Without a word to send, `tx` stays high, which is the idle level of the line.

## Uplink Decoder {#sec-uplink-decoder}

The uplink decoder is the heart of the node. Every time the uplink receiver receives a word, the decoder decides what to do with it. There are only three choices. It keeps the word because it belongs to this node, forwards it to the next node, or changes it and forwards it, which happens only for the count value (@sec-count-segments).

### Word Types {#sec-decoder-words}

The decoder first looks at the type of the word, which the ninth bit tells (@sec-9bit-uart). @tbl-decoder-words lists the four cases.

| **Word**                    | **Condition**                | **Action of the decoder**                                                |
|:----------------------------|:-----------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| EOP                         | `up_data == 9'h176`          | act on the finished packet, forward the EOP, close the packet            |
| SOP (any command)           | `up_data[8] == 1`, not EOP   | forward the SOP, open a new packet, remember its type                    |
| Data word inside a packet   | `up_data[8] == 0`, `in_frame` | keep, change or forward, depending on the packet type                   |
| Data word outside a packet  | `up_data[8] == 0`, no `in_frame` | ignore (not forwarded)                                              |

: Word types and the action of the uplink decoder {#tbl-decoder-words}

Any word with the ninth bit set, except the EOP, starts a packet. The decoder forwards it at once, sets `in_frame` and stores the packet type in two flags. `is_led` is 1 for the LED command 0x100, and `is_cnt` is 1 for the Count Segments command 0x160. The counters of the packet go back to 0. A new SOP also ends any packet that is still open, and this is how the node recovers from a lost EOP (@sec-error-handling). If the SOP is neither 0x100 nor 0x160, both flags stay 0. All data words of such a packet are forwarded unchanged, and nothing in the node changes. This keeps the design open for new commands, because a node that does not know a command simply passes it on. The EOP is the moment when the node acts on the packet. Only here are new LED levels or a new ID taken over, and only if the packet was correct. The EOP is then forwarded, and `in_frame` goes back to 0. @fig-decoder-flow and @fig-decoder-eop show the whole decision for one word, with the LED and the count logic.

![Flow of the uplink decoder for one received word. Blue boxes forward a word to the next node, green boxes keep data, and the red box marks a wrong count packet.](images/ch5_decoder_flow){#fig-decoder-flow width=80%}

The flowchart follows the code word by word. The decoder checks for the EOP first, because the EOP 0x176 also has its ninth bit set and would otherwise open a new packet. Any other word with the ninth bit set opens a new packet and resets all packet flags and counters. A data byte inside a packet then goes one of three ways. The first eight bytes of an LED packet are kept. The first byte of a count packet is stored in `temp_id` and forwarded as the value plus one, unless it is 0xFF. Every other byte is forwarded unchanged, and a second byte in a count packet marks that packet as invalid. @fig-decoder-eop shows what happens at the EOP. An EOP outside a packet is ignored. Inside a packet the node makes two checks before it forwards the EOP. It takes over the LED levels only if all eight own bytes have arrived, and it takes over the new ID only if exactly one count value has arrived. Each successful check sends a pulse to the downlink logic, which then builds the answer (@sec-downlink). In the code both checks happen in the same clock cycle. The flowchart shows them one after the other only to make them easier to read.

![Handling of the EOP in the uplink decoder. Green boxes take over new values and start an answer.](images/ch5_decoder_eop){#fig-decoder-eop width=70%}

### LED Data Packet {#sec-decoder-led}

In an LED packet the node keeps the first eight data bytes and forwards all others. The decoder counts the kept bytes in `keep_count`. While this count is below `MY_BYTES` = 8, each data byte is pushed into the 64-bit register `frame_data` from the right (@lst-decoder-keep).

```{.verilog #lst-decoder-keep lst-cap="Keeping the own data bytes of an LED packet"}
if (is_led && keep_count < MY_BYTES) begin
    // mine, push in from the right
    frame_data <= {frame_data[55:0], up_data[7:0]};
    keep_count <= keep_count + 4'd1;
end
```

After eight bytes, the first byte has moved to the top of the register. The master sends each 16-bit value with the high byte first and in the order red, green, blue and white. The four values therefore sit in fixed places of `frame_data` (@tbl-frame-data).

| **Bytes received** | **Position in `frame_data`** | **LED level**  |
|:-------------------|:-----------------------------|:---------------|
| 1 and 2            | bits 63 … 48                 | `level_red`    |
| 3 and 4            | bits 47 … 32                 | `level_green`  |
| 5 and 6            | bits 31 … 16                 | `level_blue`   |
| 7 and 8            | bits 15 … 0                  | `level_white`  |

: Position of the own data bytes in the register `frame_data` {#tbl-frame-data}

Once `keep_count` has reached 8, every further data byte belongs to a node further down the chain and is forwarded. This simple rule is why the same code works on every node. The first node keeps the first eight bytes. The second node receives the packet without these bytes, so it again keeps its "first" eight bytes, and so on down the chain.

At the EOP, the new values are copied from `frame_data` into the four LED level registers, but only if all eight bytes have arrived (@lst-decoder-eop).

```{.verilog #lst-decoder-eop lst-cap="Taking over the LED levels at the EOP"}
if (in_frame && is_led && keep_count == MY_BYTES) begin   // got all my 8 bytes
    level_red   <= frame_data[63:48];
    level_green <= frame_data[47:32];
    level_blue  <= frame_data[31:16];
    level_white <= frame_data[15:0];
    led_done    <= 1'b1;    // only answer after a good frame
end
```

The pulse `led_done` tells the downlink logic to send an LED answer (@sec-downlink). If the packet ended before all eight bytes arrived, the old levels stay active and the node does not answer.

## Cut-Through Forwarding {#sec-forwarding}

Every word that the decoder does not keep goes on to the next node, one word at a time. A word is sent on as soon as it has been received, without waiting for the rest of the packet. This is cut-through forwarding, and @sec-req-timing showed that it is the only way to meet the 25 ms limit for 25 segments.

### Forwarding Path {#sec-forwarding-path}

The forwarding path has three steps (@fig-forwarding-path). For every word that must be forwarded, the decoder puts the word on `fwd_data` and sets `fwd_valid` for one clock cycle. This pulse writes the word into the uplink FIFO `u_up_q`, which has room for eight 9-bit words. A one-line control block then reads the FIFO whenever a word is waiting and the transmitter is free (@lst-up-send).

![Forwarding path of the uplink. Words that are not kept go through the FIFO to the uplink transmitter.](images/ch5_forwarding_path){#fig-forwarding-path width=100%}

```{.verilog #lst-up-send lst-cap="Control of the uplink transmitter"}
always @(posedge clk_sys)
    up_send <= !up_q_empty && !up_busy && !up_send;   // something waiting + transmitter free
```

The term `!up_send` makes `up_send` a pulse of one cycle, so each word is read from the FIFO exactly once.

The FIFO is needed because the receiver and the transmitter are not exactly in step. Both work at 1 MBaud, so on average a word leaves the node as fast as it arrives. But the next word can be complete while the transmitter is still busy with the previous one, because the transmitter started a little later. The FIFO holds the word for this short time. In normal operation it holds at most one or two words, so a depth of eight gives a safe margin.

@fig-flexlink-forwarding shows the effect on a whole packet (Two nodes). GM1 receives the full packet, keeps its eight bytes and forwards the SOP, the eight bytes of GM2 and the EOP. GM2 therefore receives a shorter packet in which its own data is again at the start.

![LED data packet as received by GM1 from the master (top) and as forwarded by GM1 to GM2 (bottom). GM1 keeps its own eight data bytes and forwards all other words.](images/ch5_flexlink_packet){#fig-flexlink-forwarding width=100%}

### Forwarding Delay {#sec-forwarding-delay}

The delay of one node is the time from the start bit of a word at `up_rx` to the start bit of the same word at `up_tx`. Most of it is the receiving itself, because the word is ready only in the middle of its stop bit, 10.5 bit times after the start bit (@sec-uart-rx). A few clock cycles are then added by the synchronizer, the decoder, the FIFO, the control block and the output register of the transmitter.

$$
t_\text{fwd} = 10.5 \cdot T_\text{bit} + n \cdot T_\text{clk}
$$ {#eq-fwd-delay-rtl}

In the simulation of the final design the delay is 10.65 µs. The processing therefore adds only about 0.15 µs, or 7 to 8 clock cycles (@sec-hw-chain). The receiving part cannot be made shorter, because a node can only decide what to do with a word once the whole word has arrived. With store-and-forward, the first of 25 nodes alone would add the whole remaining packet of $(8 \cdot 24 + 2) \cdot 11\ \mu\text{s} \approx 2.1\ \text{ms}$.

## Count Segments {#sec-count-segments}

All nodes run the same bitstream, so after power-up no node knows its place in the chain. To give every node its own ID, the master sends a Count Segments packet to first node. Each node takes the received value as its new ID, forwards the value plus one to the next node.

### Procedure {#sec-count-procedure}

After power-up every node has the ID 0xFF. The master sends `160 | 00 | 176`. GM1 receives the value 00, remembers it as its new ID and forwards 01. GM2 then receives `160 | 01 | 176`, remembers 01 and forwards 02, and so on along the chain. At the EOP each node takes over its new ID and answers with `1B0 | my_id | 176` (@sec-downlink). The master receives one answer per node, and the IDs tell it how many nodes the chain has. @fig-count-segments shows this for the two nodes of the prototype.

![Count Segments with two nodes. Each node takes the received value as its ID and forwards the value plus one. Both nodes answer in chain order.](images/ch5_count_segments){#fig-count-segments width=100%}

@lst-count shows the part of the decoder that handles the count value. It runs only for the first data byte of a Count Segments packet.

```{.verilog #lst-count lst-cap="Handling of the count value in the uplink decoder"}
else if (is_cnt && !cnt_got) begin
    cnt_got <= 1'b1;
    temp_id <= up_data[7:0];        // wait till EOP, take it only if packet is ok
    if (up_data[7:0] != 8'hFF) begin
        fwd_data  <= {1'b0, up_data[7:0] + 8'd1};   // next GM gets +1
        fwd_valid <= 1'b1;
    end
end
```

### Safety Rules {#sec-count-rules}

The master uses the IDs to tell the answers of the nodes apart, so a wrong or double ID must never happen. The design follows three rules for this.

The new ID is taken over only at the EOP. The received value first waits in `temp_id` and moves into `my_id` only if the packet held exactly one data byte. A second data byte sets the flag `cnt_extra` and makes the packet invalid. A packet without an EOP never reaches this step. In all these cases the node keeps its old ID and does not answer.

The value 0xFF is not counted further. Adding one to 0xFF would give 0x00, and a node further down would get the same ID as the first node. A node that receives 0xFF therefore takes this value itself but forwards no count value. The next node receives a packet without a value and keeps its old ID. Since 0xFF also means "not counted yet", one byte can count up to 255 nodes.

The value is replaced, not added. The node puts the new value in place of the old one, so the packet keeps its length of three words at every node. The forwarding delay is then the same as for an LED packet.

## LED Registers and PWM Generator {#sec-pwm-generator}

We now have received the LED data and stored it in `frame_data`. The next step is to show the light on the LEDs. This is done by the four level registers and the PWM generator.

### LED Level Registers {#sec-led-registers}

The four 16-bit registers `level_red`, `level_green`, `level_blue` and `level_white` hold the brightness that the node shows. They are written only at the EOP of a complete LED packet (@lst-decoder-eop). Between two packets they keep their values, so the LEDs show the same light until the master sends new values. This covers the part of R5 that concerns the time between packets. After power-off the values are lost, and at power-up all levels are 0.

The level registers are kept apart from `frame_data` on purpose. During a packet, `frame_data` fills byte by byte while the levels still hold the old values. All four colours then change together at the EOP. A half-updated colour can therefore never appear. The latch in the Simulink model served the same purpose (@sec-sim-latch).

### PWM Generator {#sec-pwm-counter}

The PWM generator uses one free-running 16-bit counter for all four channels. The counter `pwm_counter` counts up by one in every clock cycle and goes back to 0 after 65,535. One PWM period therefore lasts 65,536 cycles.

$$
f_\text{PWM} = \frac{50\ \text{MHz}}{65{,}536} \approx 762.9\ \text{Hz}
$$

For each colour, a comparator checks in every cycle whether the counter is still below the level. While it is, the output is 1 (@lst-pwm).

```{.verilog #lst-pwm lst-cap="PWM generator with one shared counter and one comparator per channel"}
reg [15:0] pwm_counter = 16'd0;
always @(posedge clk_sys)
    pwm_counter <= pwm_counter + 16'd1;

always @(posedge clk_sys) begin
    pwm_red   <= pll_locked && ((level_red   == 16'hFFFF) || (pwm_counter < level_red));
    pwm_green <= pll_locked && ((level_green == 16'hFFFF) || (pwm_counter < level_green));
    pwm_blue  <= pll_locked && ((level_blue  == 16'hFFFF) || (pwm_counter < level_blue));
    pwm_white <= pll_locked && ((level_white == 16'hFFFF) || (pwm_counter < level_white));
end
```

A channel with the level $v$ is on for $v$ clock cycles, so its duty cycle is

$$
D = \frac{v}{65{,}536}
$$ {#eq-rtl-duty}

The level 16,384, for example, gives an output of 1 for 16,384 of 65,536 cycles. This is a duty cycle of 25 % and an on-time of $16{,}384 \cdot 20\ \text{ns} \approx 328\ \mu\text{s}$ per period.

Two levels need special care. The level 0 gives an output that is always 0, because the counter is never below 0. The highest level 65,535 needs an extra rule. Without it, the output would drop to 0 for one cycle in every period, when the counter itself reaches 65,535. The term `level == 16'hFFFF` keeps the output at 1 in this case, so 65,535 really means "always on". The price is that the levels 65,534 and 65,535 differ by two cycles instead of one, This difference is visible on the oscilloscope as a 40 ns drop in every period, but not in the brightness of the LED.

## Downlink with Answers and Temperature {#sec-downlink}

The downlink carries the answers of the nodes back to the master. Each node has two tasks here. It sends its own answer after a correct packet, and it passes on the answers of all nodes behind it. Both tasks share one transmitter, `u_dn_tx`.

### Answer Packets {#sec-answer-packets}

A node answers after every correct LED packet and after every correct Count Segments packet (@tbl-answers).

| **Trigger**                 | **Answer packet**                 | **Words** |
|:----------------------------|:----------------------------------|:----------|
| correct LED packet          | `180 | my_id | temperature | 176` | 4         |
| correct Count Segments packet | `1B0 | my_id | 176`           | 3         |

: Answer packets of a node {#tbl-answers}

The temperature is the parameter `MY_TEMP` with the fixed value 40 (0x28), because no sensor is connected in this prototype. The answer format is already complete, so a real sensor value can later take its place without any change to the protocol.

The answer is built word by word. The counter `reply_w` points to the next word, and the signal `reply_word` selects the word for this position (@lst-reply-word).

```{.verilog #lst-reply-word lst-cap="Selection of the answer word"}
wire [2:0] reply_last = reply_is_cnt ? 3'd2 : 3'd3;   // index of my EOP

wire [8:0] reply_word =
    (reply_w == 3'd0)       ? (reply_is_cnt ? CNT_DN_SOP : LED_DN_SOP) :
    (reply_w == 3'd1)       ? {1'b0, my_id} :
    (reply_w == reply_last) ? FL_EOP :
                              {1'b0, MY_TEMP};
```

For an LED answer `reply_last` is 3, so the words are SOP, ID, temperature and EOP. For a count answer it is 2, and the temperature word is left out.

### Order of the Answers {#sec-answer-order}

The answers of all nodes share one line, so they must not mix. If a word of GM2's answer appeared in the middle of GM1's answer, the master could read neither of them. The downlink logic therefore follows one simple rule. A packet that has started is always finished first.

@fig-downlink-flow shows the complete downlink logic. In every clock cycle it first checks the two pulses from the uplink decoder. `led_done` starts an LED answer and `cnt_done` starts a count answer. Both set `reply_pending` and reset the word counter `reply_w` to 0. When the transmitter is free, the logic makes one decision. If its own answer is waiting and it is not in the middle of passing on another packet, it sends the next word of its own answer. The word depends on `reply_w`. Word 0 is the SOP, word 1 is the ID and the last word is the EOP. In an LED answer word 2 is the temperature `MY_TEMP`. After its own EOP, `reply_pending` goes back to 0 and the answer is done. Otherwise, if the downlink FIFO holds a word from the next node, the logic passes this word on. The flag `passing_packet` stays 1 until the EOP of that packet has been sent, so the own answer can never start in the middle of it.

![Flow of the downlink logic in every clock cycle. Green boxes start an answer, red boxes send a word on the downlink.](images/ch5_downlink_flow){#fig-downlink-flow width=85%}

In practice the own answer comes first, because a node finishes the uplink packet before the nodes behind it. GM1 receives the EOP about 10.65 µs before GM2, so it starts its answer before GM2's answer arrives. The words of GM2's answer that arrive in the meantime wait in the FIFO, and GM1 passes them on after its own EOP. The master therefore receives the answers in the order of the chain, first GM1 and then GM2 (@fig-downlink-order).

![Order of the answers on the downlink of GM1. GM1 sends its own answer first. The answer of GM2 waits in the downlink FIFO and is passed on afterwards.](images/ch5_downlink_order){#fig-downlink-order width=100%}

The FIFO is deep enough for this. Words from the next node arrive at the same rate as they are sent, so the backlog grows only while the node sends its own answer. This is at most four words for an LED answer, which fits into the eight places of the FIFO. Every node in a longer chain works the same way, so the backlog does not grow from node to node.

## Error Handling {#sec-error-handling}

A light segment in an aircraft must never show wrong or random light because of one bad packet. The design therefore checks the packets at several levels and follows one rule. If a packet is not complete and correct, nothing changes. The node takes over no new values, keeps its ID and does not answer. A missing answer is visible to the master, so the master can find out that a packet was lost and send it again. @tbl-error-cases lists the cases that the design handles. Each of them was checked in simulation (@sec-rtl-verification). Only the errors in the content of a packet, such as a wrong length, a wrong count value or a missing EOP, were tested on the hardware (@sec-hw-robustness).

| **Error case**                        | **Detected by**                                  | **Behaviour of the node**                                   |
|:--------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|
| Short glitch on the line              | START state, line high again after half a bit    | no word received                                            |
| Broken frame (stop bit = 0)           | STOP state of the receiver                       | word dropped, no `valid`                                    |
| Data word outside a packet            | `in_frame` = 0                                   | word ignored, not forwarded                                 |
| EOP outside a packet                  | `in_frame` = 0                                   | EOP ignored, not forwarded                                  |
| LED packet too short (< 8 own bytes)  | `keep_count` ≠ 8 at the EOP                      | old levels kept, no answer                                  |
| Lost EOP, new SOP arrives             | new SOP restarts the packet                      | open packet dropped, new packet handled normally            |
| Count packet without value            | `cnt_got` = 0 at the EOP                         | old ID kept, no answer                                      |
| Count packet with more than one value | `cnt_extra` = 1                                  | old ID kept, no answer                                      |
| Count value 0xFF                      | value check before forwarding                    | node takes 0xFF, no value forwarded                         |
| Unknown command                       | `is_led` = `is_cnt` = 0                          | packet forwarded unchanged, no change in the node           |

: Error cases handled by the Flexlink node {#tbl-error-cases}

Some errors cannot be found, because the packet still has the right format. If one bit of a brightness byte flips on the line, the stop bit and the packet structure are still correct, so the wrong value is shown. If the master sends one value too many for an earlier node, all later nodes take bytes that were meant for their neighbour. Both errors could be found with a checksum for each segment, which the master adds and the node checks before it takes over the values. A first version of this idea was tried during the work, but it is not part of the final design. @sec-outlook discusses it as an extension.

The design has no reset signal. All registers get their start values from the bitstream when the FPGA is configured (@sec-clock-reset). If a node ever ends up in a wrong state, the next SOP brings the decoder back to a defined state, because every SOP sets all packet flags and counters back to their start values.

## Verification by Simulation {#sec-rtl-verification}

Before the design went onto the FPGA, it was checked in simulation with the open-source simulator Icarus Verilog [@icarus_verilog] (@sec-simulation). The testbench `tb_flexlink_node.v` connects two nodes in a chain, exactly as on the hardware, and adds a third UART receiver that plays the PC. A task in the testbench sends 9-bit words at 1 MBaud to GM1, and the testbench records every word that GM1 sends back on its downlink. The `CC_PLL` primitive of the GateMate cannot be simulated with Icarus Verilog. The testbench therefore contains a small stand-in module with the same name and ports. It passes the 50 MHz test clock straight through and reports the PLL as locked at once. Everything else is simulated exactly as it is synthesized. The testbench checks itself. For each test it compares the received answers and the on-times of the PWM outputs with the expected values and counts the errors. At the end it prints PASS or FAIL. @tbl-sim-tests lists the five tests.

| **Test** | **Stimulus**                                      | **Expected result**                                             | **Result** |
|:---------|:--------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------|
| 1        | LED packet before Count Segments                  | answers `180 0FF 028 176` twice (both nodes still have ID 0xFF) | PASS       |
| 2        | Count Segments `160 000 176`                      | answers `1B0 000 176 1B0 001 176`, IDs 0 and 1, GM2 lights D5   | PASS       |
| 3        | LED packet with 16 data bytes                     | both nodes show their own values and answer                     | PASS       |
| 4        | short LED packet with 12 data bytes               | only GM1 updates and answers, GM2 keeps its old values          | PASS       |
| 5        | packet with the unknown command 0x170             | no change, no answer, IDs unchanged                             | PASS       |

: Tests of the self-checking testbench and their results {#tbl-sim-tests}

In test 3, GM1 receives the levels 65,025, 11,025, 32,400 and 0, and GM2 receives 0, 0, 65,535 and 10,000. The testbench measures the on-time of each PWM output in clock cycles over one period and finds exactly these values. For the level 65,535 it counts 65,536 cycles, which confirms that this level is always on. Test 4 shows the rule of @sec-decoder-led. GM1 receives its eight bytes and updates, while GM2 receives only four bytes, keeps its old values and does not answer.

A second testbench, `tb_flexlink_errors.v`, uses the same chain and sends all error cases of @tbl-error-cases, such as wrong count packets, short or broken LED packets, a short glitch and a broken stop bit. It also measures the forwarding delay from the falling start edge at GM1 to the falling start edge at GM2. Depending on where this edge falls within one clock cycle, the delay is between 10.64 µs and 10.66 µs, which gives the 10.65 µs used in @sec-forwarding-delay. The results of this testbench were the expected answers for the hardware tests in @sec-hw-robustness. The testbench runs with the script `sim.bat`. It writes no waveform file, because all checks happen inside the testbench and appear as text. This makes it quick to repeat every test after each change of the code.
